en: The Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī Sūtra, translated by Li Wuchan, a Great Chieftain of the Brahmins from Northern India.
Chapter One: The Chapter on Praise. In total, there are sixteen chapters; excluding the Fundamental Great Dhāraṇī, there are twenty-seven dhāraṇīs in all.

In all the dhāraṇīs following the first, the *Sarvavidyāpati-Amoghapāśeśvararāja*, the two characters "namo" are both to be pronounced with the upper tone (level tone), while the small-character annotations are written according to the original text and should not be treated as part of the main lines; these are merely phonetic guides.
The dhāraṇī mantra is as follows:

Namaḥ ratnatrayāya | Namah amitābhāya | Tathāgatāya | Namah ārya-avalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya | Tadyathā | Oṃ | Amogha-pratihatā | Huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā | This is called the Secret Sovereign King of Unfailing Power Dhāraṇī, the Lord of All Mantras.
If one upholds and recites this mantra, it is equivalent to having recited all vidyā-mantras,
and one will be fully capable of accomplishing all activities.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara...
Furthermore, the Heart Mantra of Amoghapāśa is taught,
known as the Dharma of Unfailing Accomplishment;
it is fully capable of purifying and eliminating the accumulated karmic obstacles of immeasurable and boundless worlds.
Increasing immeasurable stores of merit and roots of goodness,
they are all able to give rise to boundless wisdom;
their spheres of supernormal power transcend and enter [the mundane].
Through skillful means, they fulfill the six pāramitās and increase all the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) of a bodhisattva,

as well as the non-empty Buddha-dharmas, the four noble truths, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the causes and conditions, liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
It enables those who behold it to cultivate and achieve the wisdom, majestic power, and strength of the stages of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas;
and to become fully endowed with intelligence, merit, auspiciousness, diligence, vigor, power, and eloquence.
He ascends into the sky and conceals his form, possessing the rank of a sovereign mantra-holding immortal.
He is endowed with worldly pleasures, abundant wealth, and nobility,
and has accomplished the methods of the auspicious vase and the wish-fulfilling jewel.
The *Kṛṣṇa-jaṭī* (Black Matted-Hair) subdues [all afflictions].
It emerges from hidden treasures (*nidhi*) and enters caves;
the *Aśana* medicine can completely cure all diseases and eliminate possession by malevolent spirits.
The method for binding the altar through mantras subdues all dragons,
as well as men, women, boys, and girls;
it prays for rain, stops rain, and brings about the extinction and subjugation of calamities and pestilence.
It can accomplish all matters,
generate all merit, and extinguish all transgressions;
it brings about the accomplishment of the *Dhāraṇī-samādhi* of boundless gates.
One shall attain the most supreme and vast Dharma.
This Great Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī King Dharma is constantly [resorted to] by all devas,
nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.
It is worshipped by bhūtas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasas,
the seven luminaries, the various lunar mansions, vināyakas, bhiñjanas, and others.
Those who prostrate to and praise it shall all be called auspicious.
It is constantly protected by Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protecting Four Kings,
and the assemblies of accomplished mantra-siddhas and various ṛṣis.
Through making offerings, sympathetic joy, faithful acceptance, and empowerment,
one obtains the practice of praise and proclamation;
one reveres, honors, and makes offerings with all manner of ritual requisites.
And they remained there to offer worship and service.
Thus ends the first chapter, "Praise. 2.
Chapter Two: "The Attainment through Recitation of the King of Mantras, the Lord of Spells, Amoghapāśa. At that time, the method for recitation was further explained.
Those who wish to uphold the mantra should bathe and purify themselves, don new and clean garments,
and receive and maintain the precepts of the Bodhisattva vows.
Abiding in a mind of loving-kindness with a spirit of great compassion,
delighting in truthful speech and removing the stains of greed,
he brings benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings.
With a sincere and straightforward mind, free from flattery or crookedness,
one should aspire to merit and eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion;
know that one should always bathe as a way of repaying kindness.
Recite the dhāraṇī while remaining mindful of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, ensuring that you do not forget them.
Present extensive offerings to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
scattering flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, and applying fragrant ointments.
Adorned with garlands, banners, streamers, and parasols, one should,
before that [image], with a single-minded, firm intention and faithful resolve,
recite the mantra of the Noble Amoghapāśahṛdayarāja one hundred and eight times.
Enter the *asunyatā-dhāraṇī-samādhi*,
form the lotus mudrā, and remain silent without speaking;
then you will attain accomplishment.
The World-Honored One, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
manifests in dreams in the form of a bhikṣu or a brāhmaṇa;
or he manifests in the form of a young boy, or a king, or a great minister.
Manifesting in such a body, he praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mahāsattva!
You have now been able to uphold and protect the teachings."
Since your wishes have already been fulfilled, what more is there to seek?
Whatever wish the mantra-practitioner requires, they should seek it;
according to their desire, the mantra will achieve accomplishment.
Whatever deeds one performs shall swiftly attain accomplishment.
All karmic obstructions will be entirely extinguished.
One will forever sever all rebirths in the miserable realms of hell and the animal kingdom; this person shall obtain the purity of the eye of wisdom, and their mindfulness shall increase.
He constantly acts as a companion to all devas,
removing obstacles so that whatever tasks are undertaken may be accomplished;
he also causes those people to be courageous and diligent, so that their mantras may achieve success.
All virtuous aspirations shall be fully accomplished;
one shall not be overcome by celestial Māras, followers of external paths, or enemies,
and shall always be praised by the noble ones.
He was beloved, honored, venerated, and supported by the king, ministers, brahmins, householders,
and all other people; he was praised by everyone.
They shall eternally serve as a place of refuge for all who are terrified,
and become the object of reliance and trust for all virtuous people.
For those who constantly recite this, within their body, speech, and mind—
All accumulated evil karma will be completely extinguished.
By reciting this once, one shall obtain clothing,
food, bedding, medicine, and other necessary requisites.
All shall attain excellence and never lack for anything;
they shall obtain long life with few illnesses and little affliction.
This concludes the second chapter, "The Chapter on Receiving and Maintaining the Accomplishment."

Chapter Three: The Chapter on Attaining Vision through the Mantra-King of the Lord of Spells, Amoghapāśa. If one wishes to behold Avalokiteśvara face-to-face, they should proceed to a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*).
Whether at a monastery in a forest hermitage where there is a stupa,
or in a garden, or by a riverbank,
or in a mountain forest— having gone to such a place as these.
He upholds the fast and precepts and the bodhisattva discipline;
he is pure in the three wheels within the three maṇḍalas;
and he enters the samādhi-dhāraṇī.
Wearing new, clean robes and dwelling in the four Brahma-abodes,
he joyfully solicited alms from the Venerable One;
having solicited them with joy, [he departed].
First, one should make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Once the offerings are completed,
in a secluded and quiet place, within a clean chamber—
Using *kuśa* grass— known as auspicious grass— as a seat,
sit upon it and recite the heart-mantra of the Amoghapāśahṛdayarāja without wavering.
Truly, do not entertain other thoughts, continuing day and night.
Even when terrifying sounds emerge from the sky,
the mantra-practitioner should not be afraid and should not leave their seat;
they should wait until musical sounds are heard from the sky.
Upon hearing its sound, one should not be startled or alarmed,
nor should one look upon it; one should simply recite the mantra until the sky rains down exquisite *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers.
One should not even give rise to thoughts of the red lotus, the blue lotus, the white lotus, or the *pāṭala* flower;
this continues until Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva himself utters words of praise.
Excellent, excellent, O mantra-holding ṛṣi!
You have already made offerings to and served me.
Since you have now fully accomplished this mantra, what further do you seek?
At that time, one should arise and,
before the World-Honored One, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
offer incense, flowers, and food of the finest quality.
Having made offerings of raw non-glutinous rice and so forth,
and having circumambulated [the deity] clockwise, one should prostrate at the feet and request, saying:
"I shall seek that which I desire according to my aspirations."
All these constitute its accomplishment.
The Chapter on the Accomplishment of Vision is concluded. 4.
The Chapter on the Ritual for the Image-Accomplishment of the King of Mantras, the Lord of Spells, the Amoghapāśa. At that time, the ritual method for fashioning the image was further expounded.
One should instruct the artist to observe the eight precepts and maintain pure fasting. Then,
upon a piece of pure white cotton cloth that has not been cut,
one should paint an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Among the various pigments used, glue must not be added.
The hair should be fashioned into a topknot, colored like the interior of a lotus.
There are three eyes on the face, and the body is draped with white gauze.
He wears a black deerskin as a sash tied around his waist;
his body has four arms,
and in the upper left hand he holds a lotus flower.
The lower left hand holds a water vessel (*kundikā*);
the upper right hand holds a rosary (*akṣamālā*);
and the lower right hand hangs downward, performing the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*).
Wearing exquisite celestial garments and all manner of ornaments to adorn his body,
he stands upon a lotus flower,
his crown resplendent with hundreds of thousands of rays of light.
He scattered various flowers to endow him with majestic power;
he adorned his body with crescent-shaped necklaces,
earrings, armlets, and bracelets.
He was adorned with a joyful countenance,
holding Amitābha Buddha upon his crown;
having fashioned this image, he—
On the eighth or fifteenth day of the waxing moon,
on an auspicious lunar mansion day, under a cloudless and windless sky,
either during the spring season or the autumn season.
First, prepare a clean area outside the city,
removing tiles, stones, thorns, bones,
and other refuse; the ground should be level, neither high nor low.
The ground there is white, or covered with green grass;
it is a place where various flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and dense forests flourish in abundance,
and where flowing springs and bathing pools are found everywhere.
Construct a square altar and spread it with powders of five colors, painting them beautifully.
Regarding the five colors: first, blue;
second, yellow; third, red; fourth, white; and fifth, the color of pale grass.
That is to say, using lime, red earth, yellow gold-essence, and golden soil—
such five-colored powders as these—
to adorn the altar, making it with four gates.
This gate is the Gate of the Four Auspiciousnesses.

Furthermore, one should fashion a śaṅkha (here translated as "white conch") and a nandikā-śrīvatsa (the *svastika* symbol of the Western lands), as well as a full vase (*pūrṇaghaṭa*) and other such forms, using colored powders spread upon the ground to create the shape of a vase. In the center of the maṇḍala, one should construct a lotus pond.
Within the pond, various kinds of lotuses and diverse birds such as geese and wild ducks are fashioned, filling its entirety.

A sacred image is installed within that pond, which is also strewn upon the ground with colored powders and adorned with various flowers, flower garlands, powdered incense, burning incense, and unguents.
Furthermore, banners, standards, and canopies shall be erected within the mandala.
On each of the four sides of the mandala,
place a flask made of either gold, silver, copper, or earthenware.
Fill the vase with pure water.

Furthermore, insert various branches from flowering trees into the mouth of the vase and bind them with silk cloth. Bind the branches in the vase with silk cloth, and place all medicinal herbs, precious gems, gold, and so forth inside the vase.
The painted vases should be made exceedingly beautiful.
Furthermore, one should scatter various flowers and rice blossoms within the mandala,
and plant many flowering trees so that they fill the entire mandala.
Hang white canopies at the four sides of the altar,
and have one person assigned to guard each side of the altar.
The mantra-practitioner shall bathe with fragrant water and don fresh, clean garments.
Three times each day, one should receive the three sets of vows and present an offering of white food before the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
namely milk, curd, ghee, honey, and so forth.
Having burned offerings of aloeswood, sandalwood, ghee, camphor, and other incenses,
the mantra-practitioner sits in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka),
forms the lotus mudrā at the heart, and joins the palms together.
Having paid homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should then recite the mantra.
The second mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amoghapratihata rākṣa rākṣa mama [insert name] huṃ phaṭ. This mantra is used to bind the topknot on the crown of the head.
The third mantra is:
Oṃ amogha-paṇṭa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. This mantra is used for binding the maṇḍala.
The fourth mantra is:
Oṃ amoghapratihata aṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ. This mantra is for binding the boundary (sīmābandha).
The fifth mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) amogha (2) ṭiṭṭibhalokeśvara (3) viśvagarama (4) hūṃ (5) phaṭ phaṭ (6). One should use this mantra to bind the boundaries of the four directions.
The sixth mantra says:
Oṃ amogarakṣa svāhā. [Recite this] to protect oneself.
The seventh mantra says:
Oṃ amogha huṃ kha. This mantra protects one’s companions.
The eighth mantra is:
Oṃ amoghadharmadhama huṃ phaṭ phaṭ. One should consecrate incense for burning with this mantra.
The ninth mantra is:
Oṃ amogha-kṛhna kṛhna hūṃ phaṭ. One should use this mantra to consecrate flowers, food, and drink before making the offering.
The tenth mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amogha-vijaye hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. When performing any rite, the mantra-holder should recite this mantra until the image of Avalokiteśvara begins to move.
The practitioner of the mantra should not fear; he should simply recite the mantra until smoke emerges, and he should likewise recite the mantra until fire blazes forth.
If it moves, one will obtain wealth; if smoke emerges, one will obtain official rank.
If the fire blazes, one will then be able to ascend into the air;
this constitutes the two methods of accomplishment.
Furthermore, while the fire is blazing, one must not rise from one's seat.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara then manifested his own form.
He comforted the mantra-practitioner and granted him whatever he required;
that person thereby attained the samādhi of a bodhisattva.
They attain non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi;
in their present bodies, they obtain the knowledge of past lives,
and further acquire immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits.
The fourth chapter, "The Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Ritual Methods," is completed. 5.

The Fifth Chapter: "The Accomplishment of the Kīlakas" (The Accomplishment of the Kīlakas of the Amoghapāśa Vidyeśvara Mantra-King). At that time, the method for accomplishing the kīlakas was further taught.
If one wishes to receive and uphold the *Kañjala*,
the Noble Amoghapāśa-kañjala shall accomplish all tasks whatsoever.
He assumes the form of a yakṣa youth,
with a wrathful face and angry eyes; his hair is reddish-yellow,
bristling upward like flames.
With a protruding nose and dog-like fangs extending upward,
he sticks out his tongue to lick his lips; his body has two arms,
and he wears blue garments while holding a rope.
Adorned with all manner of ornaments,
one should paint its image upon a cloth of hemp.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should observe the eightfold precepts.
During that night, one should go to a crossroads or place the painting in an empty room,
making offerings of flowers, flower garlands, powdered incense, burning incense, and unguents, while personally protecting oneself.
Aside from flesh and blood, one should offer all other food, drink, and requisites as an offering.
Having completed the offerings,
one should recite the King of Mantras, the Amoghapāśa, one hundred and eight times before him.
At that time, Kinkara appeared before him;
he followed whatever instructions were given and acted according to his commands.
If he was required to be dispatched to inquire about matters, he did so.
He immediately went to that place and reported exactly what he had seen and heard as it truly was. If [the king] did not then command him [to act],
[he would remain].
He shall provide one hundred coins daily to the mantra-holder.
Having received them, he should use them for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
he should not be stingy, nor should he speak of this to others.
One must not harbor hatred or disdain, nor treat them with impurity.
One should constantly make offerings, providing whatever food one has prepared.
Whenever one eats, one must always first set aside a portion of the food and give it to them.
The flavor of whatever one drinks should also first be offered;
one must never forget this.
One should avoid greed, hatred, and delusion, and abandon them all.
One should always speak truthful words and words of the Dharma,
so as not to be censured or disparaged by the noble ones.
Toward all sentient beings, one should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit.
You should single-mindedly and reverently serve Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and think of nothing else.
Constantly offer various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, flower garlands, and ointment incense.
One should also constantly recognize their kindness and repay it by making offerings of clothing, banners, canopies, and pennants.
In this manner, there were five hundred such retinues every day.
They will always have an abundance of all kinds of food, drink, requisites, flower garlands,
and scented ointments throughout their entire lives, never lacking anything;
and whenever they wish to go anywhere, they will be able to go there.
Whatever objects are required can be brought forth; this constitutes accomplishment.
The fifth chapter on the *Kinkara* ritual is hereby concluded.
6. Chapter Six: The Accomplishment of the *Citicā* Ritual, the King of Mantra-Sovereigns of the Amoghapāśa. At that time, the *Citicā* ritual is further expounded.
If one wishes to practice the *cīṭikā* rite,
that person should fashion an image of Amoghapāśa-cīṭikā in the form of a youth with an expression of joy.
His head is adorned with five topknots and all manner of ornaments;
he is born from the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
and may be fashioned from wood or white sandalwood.
Alternatively, one may use red sandalwood, fragrant sandalwood, or celestial wood;
or else use gold, silver, or paintings on silk to accomplish this.
One should wear robes of deep crimson using *hukāñjika* (bezoar);
one must not use glue.
Use vermilion mixed with the roots of *kunkuma* and *kunkuma* (saffron) itself.
One should paint his physical form so as to please the mind;
he is depicted with a joyful, smiling face, of yellowish-white complexion,
and possessing two arms, one of which holds an āmalaka fruit.
Holding a flower in one hand,
having fashioned this image and observed the fast while abiding in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
one should install it within one's own room.
Having completed the offerings of various kinds of flowers, powdered incense,
burning incense, unguents, flower garlands,
food, drink, lamps, and so forth, one stands before him.
One should recite the mantra of the King of Amoghapāśa one thousand and eight times, and then accomplishment will be attained.
The manifestation of Citika will also appear before one, whereby one shall obtain mastery.
They act immediately according to whatever instructions they are given;
whatever they see or hear, they all come to report;
and wherever they are dispatched, they receive the teachings and go or come accordingly.
They are fully capable of accomplishing all tasks that ought to be done;
they are able to bring about every benefit and can also bestow wealth.
Wherever one intends to go, they can carry one there;
they can also bring one back.
Furthermore, they will sweep and sprinkle the house where one dwells and smear the floor with mud.
He informs them of all matters so that they may know them;
he constantly speaks of auspicious things to bring them joy;
and he is able to cause all evil matters and unpleasant occurrences to be extinguished.
It can also eliminate all karmic obstructions, inauspiciousness, calamities, and epidemics, as well as all illnesses and misfortunes.
If one consumes any kind of poison, it can completely neutralize the poison so that the poison cannot cause harm.
May all aspirations whatsoever be completely fulfilled.
May the practitioner of the mantra always accumulate all provisions of merit and virtue.
May all karmic obstacles and hindrances be entirely extinguished.
Just as a loyal and filial son receives his father’s instructions and commands, there is no difference between them; whatever he desires, he shall be granted.
Likewise, if that mantra-holder constantly desires happiness and benefit, [he shall obtain them].
Do not give rise to thoughts of hatred or aversion, nor should you treat them with contempt.
Maintain purity of body by constantly bathing;
always recite [mantras], always make offerings, and always speak the truth.
With a heart of loving-kindness, one should have compassion for all sentient beings;
with single-minded reverence and faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha,
one should constantly make offerings to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
One should offer various flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, garlands,
and other such items. Furthermore, one should constantly make offerings to the Caitya,
and always provide food and drink when eating oneself.
First, set aside a portion of food to give to the Caitya;
furthermore, offer flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and so forth to the Caitya.
One must not neglect this for even a single day, but should always maintain mindfulness of it.
If it were not so, even if one were to attain the accomplishment of the dharma, they would not be subject to command;
they would simply vanish of their own accord and be unable to manifest or submit,
nor would they go away to perform any task.
Therefore, those who uphold mantras should never be negligent;
they should always diligently seek the truth without indolence,
and zealously seek the reception of the Dharma and great wisdom.
Do not allow the bodhicitta to be forgotten or lost.
You should practice in accordance with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Remain free from the defilement of greed and always stand in awe of future lives.
Constantly maintaining a sense of shame and remorse, always remaining in meditative concentration,
and upholding all mantra methods and the like—
thus, the accomplishment will ultimately never differ.
The sixth chapter, "The Chapter on the *Cīrikā*," is completed. 7.

The Seventh Chapter: The Method for Accomplishing the Auspicious Vase (*Bhadraghaṭa-sādhana*) from the *Amoghapāśa-mantra-rāja*. At that time, the method for consecrating the auspicious vase with mantras was further explained.
If one wishes to receive and uphold [the mantra], the practitioner of the dhāraṇī should first seek out virtuous people to serve as companions.
Having first established themselves in accordance with the Dharma within the ten paths of wholesome action,
they may thereafter enter all palaces or empty rooms.
In a forested area, a secluded place devoid of people,
or at a site where people attained the Way in the past,
one should construct a ritual altar within it, making it perfectly level and even.
Having purified the body by bathing and donned fresh, clean garments,
one should observe the auspicious fast, partake of milk and barley,
and protect one's companions before plastering the mandala.
One should mark out the boundaries using powdered incense leaves, realgar, red earth, and red sandalwood.
The mandala should be square, with four gates opened.
In the four directions, they take the form of the Four Heavenly Kings,
their bodies adorned with armor and all manner of ornaments,
and holding swords, bows, and arrows.
Furthermore, one should fashion various weapons on the four sides:
in the east, one should fashion a vajra;
in the south, a conch shell.
In the western direction, one should fashion a round-headed vajra;

in the northern direction, one should fashion a banner-pole for Śakti with a banner tied to its top, and furthermore, in the northern direction, one should fashion objects such as a conch, a wheel, a bowl, and a lotus.
At the four corners of the altar, hang red banners and scatter flowers of various colors.
At the center of the main altar, place the auspicious vase (bhadraghaṭa),
and paint it with various colors.
Furthermore, he tied a garland of flowers around the neck of the flask;
it was filled with lotuses and water,
as well as exquisite fragrant medicines and various famous fruits.
Furthermore, the seeds of the five grains, gold, silver, precious jewels, and pearls were also placed within it.
On all four sides of the Worthy Vase, milk gruel, curd, honey cakes, and ghee cakes were arranged in rows.
Select five men who are courageous, undaunted, and possessed of majestic virtue;
they must be trustworthy individuals capable of being entrusted with responsibilities,
whom you shall bind together as companions.
Holding swords, they stand upright to guard the four directions;
let one person stand near the mantra-practitioner,
holding various weapons to serve as attendants.
And having made offerings and provided for them,
he causes them to bathe thoroughly and put on new, clean garments,
following whatever instructions the mantra-practitioner may give.
One should act immediately according to the command and never disobey it.
One should provide protection for this mantra-holder.
One should establish the maṇḍala in accordance with the Dharma.
Arrange rows of food and drink in the four directions as an offering,
with the sole exception of alcohol and meat;
within this mandala, one should place them before the auspicious vase (kalaśa).
Having spread *kuśa* grass— known as auspicious grass— as a seat,
and having sat upon the grass, one should offer scattered non-glutinous rice and incense,
and with this mantra, bind the boundaries of all directions.
The eleventh mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amoghapāśa apratihata tejoruci viśaya rākṣa rākṣa [insert one's own name here] hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. One should also use this mantra to protect oneself and one’s companions.
Then, having formed the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), one should recite the mantra of the Noble Amoghapāśahṛdayarāja one hundred and eight times.
While reciting this mantra for one day and one night:
Alternatively, one may recite it while fasting for three days and three nights;
all obstructing Vināyakas will become terrified and cease to create obstacles.
The mantra-holder must maintain a steady mind;
they should recite the mantra silently without fear or alarm,
even if the sound of a terrifying yakṣa is heard from the south.
Upon hearing this sound, take white mustard seeds and recite the mantra over them seven times;
scatter them toward that direction to oppose the sound,
and it will immediately be eliminated and stilled.
I shall never again dare to create obstacles.
As it is in the south, so it is likewise in the east, west, and north;
all obstacles shall be completely extinguished.
The twelfth mantra is:
Oṃ (1) amogha (2) apratiṣṭhita (3) hana hana (4) huṃ (5) phaṭ phaṭ (6). When this mantra is recited over the auspicious vase, it immediately moves.
When one wishes to manifest the signs of accomplishment,
the mantra-holder’s mind must not waver;
nor should they rise, nor should they intend to abandon their seat.
One should simply recite the mantra so that this auspicious flask may bring great benefit, equal to a maṇi jewel,
capable of granting all that is desired;
it is extremely difficult to receive and uphold.
If one attains accomplishment, one will possess great power;
one will be able to obtain supernatural faculties and bestow peace and happiness,
and will cause all things to be abundant and able to be accumulated.
It causes all merits to increase.
Therefore, uphold it and do not be negligent; let it not pass in vain.
If the vessel of the wise should emit fire and blaze with flames, [one should know that one's liberation is near].
Even if it should shake or move, do not be startled or alarmed.
Eventually, from the vessel, there will emerge gold, silver, mani-jewels, various kinds of necklaces, and garments of diverse colors and exquisite quality, along with various articles of adornment.
He emits exquisite, upright, and beautiful girls, boys, men, and women, as well as celestial beings endowed with excellent marks;

he emits vehicles for riding and palaces, gardens, cities, villages, streets, and great highways; he emits elephants, horses, chariots, carriages, and foot-soldiers; and he emits food and drink, incense, flower garlands, ointments, banners, parasols, and pennants.
The sounds of music and song arise;
even the mantra-holder should not rise,
until that Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara [appears].
He transformed himself into the physical form of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
as he emerged from his precious vase together with his retinue of bodhisattvas,
those who had previously emerged did so through this supernatural power.
All [the others] vanished and did not appear again;
only the retinue of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva remained present, praising him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, O mantra-holding ṛṣi!"
"You have now attained the accomplishment of this mantra;
whatever you may seek, it shall all be granted to you.
At that time, the mantra-holder immediately rose, joined his palms, circumambulated [the deity] to the right, and prostrated.
Having performed the prostrations, he addressed him, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will graciously bestow this auspicious vase upon me.
Thereupon, the Holy Bodhisattva Samantabhadra spoke these words to the practitioner of the mantra:
"You should accept and enjoy it as you wish.
Having received it, the practitioner places it upon his head and then sets it upon the ground,
where he makes offerings with flowers, incense, and flower garlands.
I shall immediately make a vow and take refuge in the World-Honored One,
so that I and my companions may fulfill all our aspirations.
Having spoken these words,
he vanished and departed to wherever he wished,
while that noble flask followed the mantra-practitioner.
The forms one desires change according to one’s will; this is the method for accomplishing the *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar).
The seventh chapter, on the Auspicious Jar, is complete.

Chapter Eight: Accomplishing the Messenger (*dūta*). Regarding the *Amoghapāśa-prakāśa-mantrādhipati*, the King of Spells, for the Chapter on Accomplishing the Messenger, the eighth: if one wishes to subjugate a messenger, [one should proceed as follows].
That mantra-practitioner shall draw a messenger in the form of a child,
adorned with all ornaments and having a joyful countenance;
his head has five topknots, and his body is pleasing to behold.
Clad in yellow garments and holding a lotus flower in his hand,
his body yellowish-white in color, he wanders through the air;
he is placed in the secret location within the vihāra.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the waxing moon,
observe the fast and precepts, bathe with fragrant water, and put on new, clean garments.
Offer various flowers and burn incense, powdered incense, and so forth.
Having made offerings of scented ointments, flower garlands, lamps, and food and drink to him,
one should sit in the full lotus posture before him and recite the Heart Mantra of the Amoghapāśa King one hundred and eight times; he will then appear before one and speak to the reciter.
"Whatever boon you seek, I shall grant it to you.
The incantation-practitioner replied,
"I now require you to serve as my attendant and receive my instructions."
He spoke thus: "Whatever commands you may give, I shall perform them all;
I shall carry out and accomplish every command from this time forward."
I shall never dare to disobey, but shall act entirely according to your instructions.
I shall always make offerings and never dare to treat you with disrespect. Whenever I wish to eat or drink, I shall always first set aside a portion of food for you.
Only after giving to them should you yourself eat; you must certainly not forget this.
If you act in this way, they will submit to you, being able to provide wealth and show you hidden treasures.
Whatever objects were required, they all brought them forward;
whatever was seen or heard, they conveyed it into his ears,
informing him and explaining it so that he might know.
They shall never lack for anything they require,
and they shall cause all past lives to be remembered,
as well as all matters of the past, future, and present.
Whatever questions may be asked, he explains them all, never failing to speak the truth.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, "The Chapter on the Messenger. 9.
The Ninth Chapter: The Treasury of Subjugation, the King of Mantras, the Lord of Illumination, the Amoghapāśa. Regarding the time when one wishes to extract hidden treasures:
First, one should protect oneself.
One should go to a cemetery and take the corpse of a man who has not yet decomposed,
whose body is without injury or burn marks.
Having bathed him,
they made offerings to that corpse with incense and flower garlands,
and rubbed its soles with ghee and oil.
He recites the mantra until the other person rises and speaks,
saying, "Noble One, what command do you have that I should carry out?
The mantra-practitioner then provides him with paper, a pen, and ink.
He caused all the locations of hidden treasures to be transcribed,
including the names of their respective regions, cities, towns, villages, and so forth, as well as the methods for extracting them;
if there were mantras to be recited, he had each one recorded in full detail.
If one does not use a written note, one should say to that person:
"You should fetch it yourself for me.
Upon hearing these words, that person will then fetch the object themselves.
Whatever objects he obtains, he shall enjoy them all;
for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, he shall practice generosity by giving them to all sentient beings.
He will then repeatedly bring precious objects [to you].
If one does not enjoy making offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the destitute,
then one will not further achieve this dharma.
If one is unable to go to the cemetery to approach a corpse that has arisen there, [one will likewise fail].
If one has previously heard of a location where a hidden treasure (nidhi) lies,
one should go to that place during the night together with a close companion who is capable of being entrusted with absolute sincerity and faith.
Avoiding transgressions and seeking merit, one should possess understanding and insight;
one should associate with those who are harmonious and virtuous as companions,
and first of all, protect oneself.
Thereafter, light a ghee lamp and recite the Amoghapāśa King Mantra one hundred and eight times.
Use śamī wood— here translated as *gouqi* (dog-rose)— as fuel to kindle the fire.
He then made this vow: "Now, for the sake of all beings so that they may forever be free from poverty, I shall dispatch him.
Thereupon, he ascended into the air and proceeded to that place of great hidden treasure, where he arrived and remained.
The fire blazes intensely and does not go out;
it remains until the mantra-holder arrives at the location of the treasury,
whereupon it only then extinguishes once he has established the boundary with certainty.
Standing upon the hidden treasure, he commands his companions to dig.
Once they have reached the spot,
he then makes offerings of milk porridge and sesame porridge to the deity of the treasure.
Then, one takes those goods and divides them into three parts:
one part for one's own use,
and the second part for the use of one's companions.
One-third of the portion should be given as an offering to the Triple Gem together with one's companions;
the portion taken for oneself should likewise be offered.
One should wish that all sentient beings may share and utilize it together.
Because it is distributed and given away from this very source, its taking is ultimately inexhaustible;
throughout the entirety of one’s lifespan, it never undergoes change.
This concludes the ninth discourse, "The Treasury of Subjugation."
Chapter Ten: Entering the Cave. Regarding the *Amoghapāśa-prabhāsa-mahārāja-mantra-rāja*, Chapter Ten: Entering the Cave.
If one wishes to enter a cave, the mantra-holder should form a partnership with virtuous persons as companions.
Having protected himself, he entered the mountain and reached the cave-dwelling; this cave was the abode of the asuras.
Within that cave, there flowed fragrant water possessed of spiritual wonders.
Those who are known by all to have previously achieved accomplishment should,
on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon,
observe the fast with purity and bathe in fragrant water.

Donning new, clean robes and performing the incense offering according to the ritual rules, one should recite the Amoghapāśarāja Dhāraṇī until the cave opens; at that time, one need not be afraid and must not cease the recitation.
Eventually, one of his female attendants appeared, holding fragrant flowers and garlands, and spoke these words:
"Welcome, O mantra-practicing rishi; please accept these fragrant flowers from me."
At that time, the mantra-holder did not respond immediately;
he waited until she had requested him three times before speaking:
"Sister, welcome! Sister, if you can accept me..."
"You may go with me as my companion.
At that time, each companion took the hand of the courtesan of his choice;
having taken her hand, she became his wife.
All that is desired shall be made fully complete.
One will act as a servant at will,
and wherever one desires to go, one is able to go there.
They are able to manifest all manner of bodily forms according to their desires;
they regain their youth, like celestial youths,
and together they engage in play and enjoy every pleasure.
Without abandoning the human body, one shall obtain a celestial body and become a mantra-siddha.
As for the practitioner of the mantra, they need only recite the mantra,
even [in the presence of] all the most excellent and noble women.
Surrounded by a retinue of five hundred, he came forth bearing garments,
fragrant ointments, and articles of adornment;
with reverent offerings and prostrations, he addressed the mantra-reciter, saying:
"Welcome, Noble One! Please accept this robe, as well as these unguents and ornaments out of compassion for me.
After he has thus requested three times, the reciter accepts them for the sake of the Dharma.
As soon as one has received [the empowerment], one vanishes along with the court ladies and no longer appears.
One becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King who upholds the mantra;
having cast off the human body, one then attains a celestial body.
Furthermore, all the vidyādhara sages and others prostrated at his feet and praised him with auspicious words;
they erected hundreds of thousands of victory banners, parasols, and streamers.
Furthermore, various kinds of music were performed,
producing exquisite sounds such that all who heard them attained celestial sovereignty, peace, and happiness.
The mind of mindfulness of the Buddha is never forgotten;
the practice of a bodhisattva likewise never ceases or is abandoned.
Having attained the knowledge of past lives, one is forever freed from the evil realms.
They shall not be intoxicated or deluded by sensual desires or wine;
they will constantly behold the Buddhas and various Bodhisattvas,
and will be fully able to bring immeasurable sentient beings to accomplishment.
Causing them to abide upon the path to bodhi,
they are able to enter samādhi and attain the dhāraṇī of non-deluded wisdom.
This concludes the tenth chapter, "Entering the Cave."

Chapter Eleven: The Accomplishment of the Anjana Medicinal Preparation, the King of Mantras, the Lord of Amoghapāśa. Regarding the accomplishment of the *añjana* medicinal preparation: if one speaks fully, it is called *suvīrāñjana*, a very heavy substance resembling silver. If one wishes to accomplish the *añjana* medicine: [The following is the ritual procedure: First, one should go to a secluded place and perform the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*). Then, one should prepare a mandala and worship the Great Compassionate One. Next, one should take a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, fill it with pure water, and place within it a single stalk of white lotus. Then, one should take the aforementioned *suvīrāñjana* and grind it with milk. Having ground it, one should place it within the vessel. Then, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. When the recitation is complete, one should take a small amount of the *añjana* and apply it to the eyes. Once applied, one will become invisible to all beings, and one will be able to travel through the sky. Furthermore, one will be able to see all the treasures hidden beneath the earth and obtain them at will. This concludes the eleventh chapter on the accomplishment of the *añjana* medicinal preparation.
The mantra-practitioner should take realgar, ox-gall, and *suvīra* and *añjana*, wrap these three substances together,
and perform this on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
Having observed the fast with purity, bathed in fragrant water, and donned new, clean garments,
one should make extensive offerings to Avalokiteśvara and call to mind all the Buddhas.
One should sit in the full lotus posture before him and recite the Heart Mantra of the Noble Amoghapāśa one hundred and eight times,
waiting until the sign of smoke emerges from within it.
Thereafter, smear the altar.
Place the medicinal packet upon a bodhi leaf.
Recite the mantra until smoke and flames arise, emitting light and causing the substance to melt.
One should know that the ritual for the accomplishment of the *āśvāsana* (soothing) medicine is now complete.
At that time, one should bind the boundary of the four directions and protect oneself.
Upon taking out the medicine, one should consecrate it with this mantra; this mantra is the thirteenth.
The thirteenth mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) amogha (2) apratihata (3) hūṃ (4) jvala (5) jvala (6) phaṭ (7) svāhā (8). Having recited the mantra, one should take *añjana* and other such substances.
Grind it together with a whetstone until it is finely powdered.
By applying this to the eyes, one will be able to see hidden treasures;
furthermore, one will attain the power of invisibility, going wherever one wishes with complete mastery over entering and exiting [any place].
There was not a single person who could see [it],
yet all were able to see all the bodhisattvas,
as well as all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas.
Furthermore, they shall also behold all sentient beings in the realms of gods, hells, and animals at the time of their birth and death;
they shall see them performing deeds of transgression and deeds of merit,
attaining mastery over all such matters.
They receive offerings;
they see all caves and all dragon palaces,
and are likewise able to manifest every kind of body.
Wherever they wish to go, they are able to travel there;
by means of the power of meditative concentration on supernormal faculties, they attain the stage of supernormal faculties and depart through them,
even unto seeing the Buddhas and receiving the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
They receive the prediction of enlightenment; they possess the most supreme wisdom and skillful means of all bodhisattvas;
they attain all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), samādhis, and masteries;
and they obtain all the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
All shall attain fulfillment and be endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*).
They shall obtain the power of all mantras and dhāraṇīs, and attain fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
This concludes the eleventh chapter, "The Chapter on the Accomplishment of Peace" (*Anśana-parivarta*).

Chapter Twelve: Prohibiting Possession by Various Ghosts and Spirits; The Sovereign Mantra-King of the Amoghapāśa. This chapter should be titled "Prohibiting Possession by Evil Ghosts and Spirits," though the translator has omitted this for brevity. If one’s mind is pure, one possesses faith, and one is diligent, [then...]
Sentient beings who have performed virtuous deeds,
those whose doubts are dispelled, those who are pure,
those who recognize their debt of gratitude, and those who resolutely seek accomplishment— namely, the bodhisattvas— shall attain success.
This is not something that can be accomplished by an ordinary lady.
For this reason, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"The mantra of the maṇi jewel is a spell for medicinal herbs."
These three kinds possess inconceivable power;
the realm of all Buddhas is inconceivable.
If one recites this mantra one hundred and eight times, [the result will be attained].
All matters will be accomplished.
One will be forever freed from all illnesses caused by attachment.
Whether for one day or two days.
If one recites this Amoghapāśa mantra for three days or seven days, the single syllable *phaṭ*—
pronounced with a half-syllable duration alone— is able to eliminate all fevers and heat-related ailments.
Recite the mantra twenty-one times over a scarlet thread,
tying one knot with each recitation until twenty-one knots are made.
When tied around [the patient], all illnesses and high fevers will be cured.
All seven celestial bodies shall provide protection;
one shall never be troubled or disturbed by them, nor shall there be untimely death.
Next, the method for reciting the mantra is explained: if one wishes to treat a fever that recurs once every four days by means of cauterization, [the following should be done].
Construct a square altar and scatter flowers upon it.
Have the patient sit facing the center of the altar.
Recite the Amoghapāśa King Mantra three times over a blade of tempered iron.
Furthermore, one should fashion the shape of that sick child out of dough and cut it with a knife;
the child will then become terrified.
If one succeeds in seeing [the deity], illnesses will be eliminated without exception. If one wishes to perform a rite of restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*) over another person,
that person should first bathe, put on new and clean garments,
and protect their own body.
Smeared with the dung of a cow, construct a square altar.
Use colors to draw the altar so that it is perfectly symmetrical and orderly.
Scatter flowers within the altar and, having made offerings of white food, perform the ritual worship.
Have either a young boy or a young girl bathe until they are pure,
dress them in clean white garments,
and adorn their bodies with various ornaments.
Have them sit cross-legged within the mandala;
bind their topknots while reciting this mantra—
specifically, the fourteenth mantra.
The fourteenth mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amogha-pratihatā rākṣa rākṣa [insert name here] svabhāvabhyo huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having filled his hands with flowers, [one should recite this].
Furthermore, scatter flowers, incense, and unhusked rice;
burn aloeswood incense while reciting the Amoghapāśa mantra.
Having recited it three times:
Scatter flowers and incense upon the face of that youth;
thus one attains the power of the *dhāraṇī*.
The fifteenth mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amogharāja pratishtita huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Furthermore, recite this mantra over water three times.
If one sprinkles [the water] upon the person's face, they will regain their speech;
whatever matters are asked about— whether auspicious or inauspicious,
whether past, future, or present— all shall be explained in full detail.
This is called the rite for restraining those who are not ill; the rite for restraining those who are ill should likewise be performed within a mandala.
One should burn aloeswood incense, scatter flowers as an offering, and have the sick person sit within the mandala.
Reciting the mantra immediately restrains it.
Grasping its middle and ring fingers and squeezing them causes it to speak;
once it has been made to take an oath, release it.
This is used for the sixteenth mantra.
The sixteenth mantra says:
Oṃ amogha-pratihatā gaccha-gaccha svabhāvanā svāhā. The seventeenth mantra says:
Oṃ amogha śāpaya hūṃ phaṭ. If [the disciple] does not release [the vow], then one should subdue and punish them by reciting this mantra over them.
By reciting this mantra, one shall release it so that it burns away and departs;
henceforth, none shall dare come here to cause affliction.
Furthermore, if one is possessed by any kind of spirit and wishes to be cured of the illness:
Recite the mantra over mustard seeds three times and strike [the patient] with them.
Furthermore, for all ghosts, those afflicted by epilepsy, or those possessed by spirits difficult to restrain,
one should perform the ritual of the *zhao* (sacrificial feast).
Smear the ground with cow dung to create an altar. Within it,
kindle a fire using branches of the Bodhi tree, Śamī wood, and Jīvaka wood as fuel.
*Apāmārga*, here translated as "ox-knee" (*niuxi*), refers to its root; this is to be mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), curd (*dadhi*), and honey.
One should recite the mantra while burning it one hundred and eight times for either one day and night or three days and nights.
Recite the Avalokiteśvara Amoghapāśa Dhāraṇī; or else,
having consecrated either mustard seeds or all kinds of seeds with the mantra, burn them.
If one is possessed by a yakṣa,
burn aloe-wood incense and mustard seeds together.
If one is possessed by a deva or nāga, [perform the same].
Burn it by mixing it with powdered sandalwood and aloeswood.
For all those who are possessed,
burn it by mixing it with sesame seeds, mustard seeds, or white mustard seeds.
Whether for one day and night or three days and nights,
by reciting the mantra once for each instance, all that is possessed shall be extinguished. Furthermore,
when all manner of calamities and pestilential diseases arise, [this shall likewise prevail].
Mix salt and milk together, consecrate them with this mantra, and burn them.
All calamities, epidemics, strife, and afflictions shall be completely extinguished.
This concludes the twelfth chapter, "On the Possession by Various Ghosts and Spirits."
13. Chapter on Entering the Mandala. This is the thirteenth exposition of the *Amoghapāśa-maṇḍala-vidhi*, the King of Mantras known as the Lord of Radiance.
It is intended for those who wish to gather all bodhisattvas and those who perceive the Mahāyāna.
One should behold the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara as being equal to seeing the Buddha, without any distinction or difference between them,
for the purpose of acquiring dhāraṇīs.
Desiring to sever the fear of falling into the evil realms,
and in order to accomplish both self-benefit and the benefit of others by attaining the auspicious paths,
one should diligently seek and rely upon a great offering maṇḍala that accords with the Dharma.
The mantra-holder, desiring to benefit all sentient beings,
should don the armor of diligence and not keep this teaching secret; rather,
they should instruct it in detail according to the words and their meaning.
Do not give rise to greed, nor harbor flattery or deception.
You should always maintain right mindfulness toward all sentient beings,
acting with equanimity and skillful means.
Do not harbor thoughts of indolence or arrogance.
Do not engage in strife, contention, or litigation.
Constantly maintain the pure precepts and bathe every day.
There are three kinds of altars:
first, the royal altar;
second, the ministerial altar.
Third, there are the altars for all commoners.
The altar for kings is established extensively;
the altar for ministers is established in the center.
If it is for an altar for all ordinary laypeople,
one should construct it according to their means as appropriate;
if it is made for a king, the intermediate method is not used.
If performing it for a minister, do not employ the lower methods;
if performing it for an ordinary person, there are no methods of addition or subtraction.
It is auspicious to perform each according to its respective ritual rules.

If one does not rely on this fundamental method, calamities will inevitably arise. O King, for a high-ranking minister it is of the superior grade, for a middle-ranking official it is of the middling grade, and for a commoner it is of the inferior grade; according to what is appropriate for each, the ritual of the mandala should be performed, for it is improper to act in a contrary manner.
When constructing a maṇḍala,
the practitioner of mantras should first select the site, discerning its auspicious or inauspicious characteristics,
and should observe that ground for one night.
Whether by a riverbank, in a mountain forest, or in a garden—
whichever place is pleasing and auspicious—
one should perform the rite of the maṇḍala at that location.
Dig deeply to remove thorns, stones, shards, and bones;
discard the old soil and fill the pit with fresh, pure earth from another location.
Once the excavation is filled, level it firmly and make it perfectly even.
It was exceedingly refined, beautiful, and level as the palm of a hand;
like a stainless mirror, it made the ground fine and smooth.
Having prepared the ground, he constructed a mandala upon it.
If it is for a king, the area should be thirty-two cubits square;
using gold, maṇi-jewels, and other such materials ground into powder,
they are mixed together to delineate the boundaries of the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, take the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—and construct five boundary-paths.
The mandala should have four gates opened, and furthermore, four auspicious gates should be fashioned.
Use branches from various trees to create flower garlands and arrange them all around.
On both sides of the eastern gate, two *śrī-mahādeva* kings should be fashioned to serve as gatekeepers:
on the right side, the King Who Protects the Nation (*Rāṣṭrapāla*) should be made;
on the left side, the King Who Increases [Merit] (*Vivardhana*) should be made.
His body is adorned with armor and all manner of ornaments;
his eyes are red and his face is wrathful, and he holds a trident in his hand.
The Protector of the Nation holds a round-headed mallet in his hand.
On both sides of the southern gate, two spirit-kings are fashioned:
the first named Chou-mu (Ugly Eyes) and the second named Chi-yen (Red Eyes).
Their bodies are adorned with ornaments of gold.
Clad in armor and wielding swords, bows, and arrows—
one of yellowish-white complexion and one of crimson complexion— with a hideous eye on the left and a red eye on the right, these two *śrīman* kings are stationed on either side of the western gate.
The first was named Maṇibhadra;
the second was named Pūrṇabhadra.
Each maintained his original clothing and appearance.
Their bodies are clad in armor,
adorned with all manner of ornaments, and they hold nooses and battle-axes;
two divine kings (śarabha-rāja) are fashioned on both sides of the northern gate.
One is named Vaiśravaṇa,
and one is named Vajrapāṇi;
each maintains his own form and wears his original garments.
Adorned with all manner of ornaments and holding ritual implements,
one should visualize Avalokiteśvara at the center of the maṇḍala,
wearing a celestial crown with dark blue hair flowing down.
Adorn his body with all manner of ornaments;
upon his head, he should visualize Amitābha Buddha and bodhisattvas the color of crystal.
Of the four arms, the upper left hand holds a lotus-vase, that is, a precious *kundikā*; the lower left hand performs the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*);
and the upper right hand grasps a rosary (*akṣamālā*).
The lower right hand performs the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*).
He is upright and exquisitely beautiful, delighting the hearts of all beings,
manifesting an expression of joy, and surrounded by a halo of light.
Adorned with the light of exquisite celestial flowers,
he forms the *svastika* (the Western script symbol) upon his chest; his eyes gaze downward as if looking askance,
and he stands upon a lotus pedestal.
To his right, one should depict the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
his form and demeanor should be serene, as described in the section on the celestial crown, though that portion is abbreviated here. His body is adorned with celestial ornaments.
Wearing celestial, exquisite robes and baring the right shoulder,
he stands with palms joined before Avalokiteśvara.
To his left, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva should be depicted.
His physical form was upright and majestic, with a complexion like that of a lotus;
he wore a precious celestial crown, his deep blue hair hung down,
and all manner of ornaments adorned his body.
Possessing two arms and a joyful countenance,
he stands before the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with his right shoulder bared and his palms joined in reverence.
Beneath Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
one should depict the Maṇicūḍa deity and the Vajra deity,
both with their two knees bent and resting upon the ground.
One should be positioned below the Bodhisattva Śrīghoṣa as the goddess Tārā and the goddess Bhṛkuṭī,
wearing celestial fine garments and adorned with celestial necklaces and bodily ornaments.
Her body is yellowish-white, her facial expression is joyful, and her demeanor is serene.
The goddess Tārā wears white garments,
while Bhṛkuṭī wears garments of various colors.
The Maṇicī and the Vajradūta deities also wore robes of various colors;
together they joined their palms and knelt with both knees upon the ground.
Gazing up at the face of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
one should perform the Amoghapāśa Mantra King beneath Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
His body is heavy and the color of jujube fruit; he has four arms and four tusks.
He wears red garments and possesses three eyes, which are red in color and emit rays of red light.
Adorned with necklaces covering the entire body and those adorning the upper half of the body,
he knelt with both knees on the ground, joined his palms in reverence,
and gazed up at the face of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
His countenance was joyful, his eyes and brows clearly defined;
his earrings were exquisite, and his mind was fixed in concentration.
He was slightly inclined forward, appearing as if about to take flight.
On both sides of the Bodhisattva were the Brahmā and Brahmā-purohita devas,
as well as the Īśvara and Maheśvara devas with their retinues;
each held garments of various colors and ornaments for adornment.
Facing the Bodhisattva, they stood with palms joined in homage.
In the four directions surrounding him were four dragon kings:
first, the Dragon King Sāgara.
Second, the Nāga King Anavatapta;
third, the Nāga King Nanda;
fourth, the Nāga King Upananda.
In the north, there are four asura kings:
the first is named King Vairocana,
and the second is named King Rāhula.
The third is King Vemacitra;
the fourth is King Bāli.

Thus, within the maṇḍala, one should fashion all the mudrās and all the weapons: the conch, wheel, lotus, nandikā, śakti, circular-headed staff, trident, noose, śakti, dundubhī, śrīvatsa, flower garland, banner, and so forth.
The various tea-leaves and flowers are collectively fashioned into a flower-canopy.
One should employ saffron, cow bezoar, realgar, gold essence, and cinnabar;
these must not be mixed with glue, and they should be painted in their pure colors.
The painting master should be granted the eightfold precepts.
Banners of various colors— blue, yellow, red, and white— should be suspended all around the four sides of the altar,
and a white canopy should be spread above.
One should employ eight vessels, whether they be of gold, silver, or red copper.
Fill these eight vessels with pure water,
and within the water place various famous incenses such as sandalwood, aloeswood, camphor, and saffron.
Having filled it with all kinds of seeds mixed together,
one should insert branches from flowering and fruit-bearing trees into the vase and tie various flower garlands around its neck.

The flowers listed above are interspersed as a floral garland; above this floral adornment, four incense jars, four incense burners, four vessels of clarified butter, and four vessels of honey are arranged in alternating rows.
There were four jars of milk and four jars of curd, all filled with various flowers, fruits, and food offerings.

Various foods and drinks were prepared by mixing them with granulated sugar, as well as syrups made by mixing sugar with water. There were also fragrant and delicious meals such as sesame porridge, barley porridge, and the like.
With the exception of alcohol, meat, and the five pungent herbs, one should wear all other [ornaments].
One should scatter various flowers, burn various incenses,
and offer flower garlands and the like.
All items required for the maṇḍala shall be arranged and distributed throughout it.
The four sides of the maṇḍala are to be surrounded by a perimeter wall,
or curtains may be hung, and musical instruments installed, all in accordance with the ritual rules.
Furthermore, one person shall be stationed in each of the four directions to serve as a guardian.
Moreover, within ten *li* of each of the four sides,
the area shall be filled with the fourfold army of infantry, elephants, cavalry, and chariots for protection.
In order to eliminate calamities and obstacles,
the king performs these auspicious rites; thereafter, he causes the king to enter the maṇḍala,
which should be sealed with hand gestures (mudrā).
The Indian tradition has already sent willow branches for purification.
One should wear clean white garments and observe the fast and precepts;
this applies to those who are trustworthy or one's own kinsmen.
Or if his brothers, sons, and so forth wish to enter the maṇḍala, they shall all receive empowerment;
mustard seeds are then tied upon their hands.
He should also provide willow branches and instruct them to observe the fast and precepts.

Following the ritual for entering the maṇḍala, he should comfort them with kind words and then lead them into the maṇḍala to seek the Master and the deity. Regarding the deity, it is the Holy One; they should make offerings of flowers, incense, lamps, food, and drink, and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
One should recite the mantra over mustard seeds and scatter them according to the ritual manual for the fast.
This mantra is used with the eighteenth incantation.
The eighteenth incantation says:
Oṃ amogha-pratihatā panta panta rākṣa rākṣa sarvasattvān hūṃ kṣiḥ aṃ phaṭ svāhā. This constitutes the nineteenth mantra for binding the boundary. It is said:

Oṃ tīrthike viśaye amoghapāśa samara samaya tiṣṭhaṇa mahāsamaya prabhadra huṃ phaṭ. In this mantra, the second phrase begins with the syllable *tī*, where the *t* is a half-syllable and the *ī* is a full syllable.
The letter *ka* consists of a full tone, while the half-tone is calculated as follows:
within the fifth phrase, *sa* is a half-tone and *ma* is a full tone;
within the seventh phrase, *śa* is a half-tone and *ṭha* is a full tone.
The ninth phrase contains the full *pātra-pāṇi*.
This serves as the mantra for binding the ritual site (*maṇḍala*).
The twentieth mantra is:
Oṃ amogha rākṣa rākṣa hūṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra for protecting oneself.
The twenty-first mantra is as follows:
Oṃ hūṃ gha dhama dhama pratyuddhava ja maviḷamba svāhā. This is called the "Mantra for Burning Incense."
The twenty-second mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) Amogha (2) Aghora (3) Puṣpapātābhivimocana (4) Cāriṇi (5) Hūṃ (6) Phaṭ (7). One should use this mantra to consecrate flowers for offering.
The twenty-third mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amogharājapratīcchakāragamadhye kṣuṇa-kṣuṇa mālini svāhā. One should consecrate the food and drink, such as cultivated non-glutinous rice, with this mantra for the purpose of making offerings.
The twenty-fourth mantra is:
Oṃ amogha upaviśa hūṃ phaṭ. When reciting this mantra, the practitioner should form the lotus mudrā and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
One must not cease the recitation of the Amoghapāśahṛdaya-mantra until one hears within the maṇḍala the sounds of confession, the snapping of fingers,
the exclamation "Excellent!", and even the scattering of flowers.
One should know that the maṇḍala has already received empowerment;
now is precisely the time to enter the maṇḍala.
The mantra-holder may rise and prostrate.
The mantra-deity then emerged, took the king by his right hand, and covered his eyes with a silk cloth.
He then caused him to prostrate before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
as well as the mantra-deity and all the other deities.
The Vajra-messenger Tārapī-koṭi-māmaki, as well as the Bodhisattvas Mahāsthāmaprāpta and Samantabhadra,
constantly perform repentance and make vows with joyful hearts and reverent faith.
Holding flowers in one's hands, one enters before the altar and scatters the flowers from the hands.
One observes where the flowers fall and upon which deity they land;
then, that deity will be able to grant accomplishment.
Prostrating with palms joined and upholding the precepts, he spoke these words:
"From this day forward, I shall no longer consume alcohol, meat, or the five pungent herbs.
Nor shall I take refuge in or prostrate before other deities."
One should always recognize kindness and repay it;
take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Bodhisattvas;
and one should single-mindedly keep the ācārya in mind.
May all the bodhisattvas, the dharma-protectors, the divine beings, the spell-deities, and others, fully know and bear witness to this:
from this day forward,
I shall bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
He causes them to receive the bodhisattva vows and makes their resolve for awakening firm;
even at the cost of their lives, they dare not commit evil or engage in sinful deeds.
One should not deceive or betray any sentient being,
causing them to take refuge in one with faith and respect;
one must never speak falsely, but always speak the truth.
Not practicing wrong conduct, relying on right view and emptiness, one does not grasp at signs.
There is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
Thus he spoke three times.
By this virtuous aspiration, may I attain Buddhahood as the Holy Honored One among two-legged beings,
and may I completely heal all the diseases of affliction of all sentient beings.
May they all likewise aspire to this same practice.
Having made this vow, one should then reveal to them the King’s Secret Seal, the Amoghapada Dhāraṇī.
Once the transmission of the dharma is completed, they shall return from the maṇḍala after a short time.
Those attendants who are to enter the maṇḍala should follow the aforementioned ritual procedures.
When about to enter or when about to exit,
the king should perform great acts of giving for the sake of the mantra-holder.
Having performed the extensive offerings, he took his leave and returned to his own palace.
This concludes the ritual for the king’s entry into the great maṇḍala.
If it is for a minister, the maṇḍala should be sixteen cubits in length and breadth.
As described above, one should fashion all the mantra-deities.
Use ordinary colors to paint the boundary altar,
and one should also properly prepare the ground.
There is no need for materials such as gold, silver, or precious gems;
the offerings, including food and drink, should be prepared according to one's means.
One should also set up banners and streamers, and place four "milk-bottle" vases.
One should offer all kinds of incense, flowers, and burning incense as offerings.
According to one's capacity, perform the empowerment ritual (*abhiṣeka*).
This is the ritual for the inner mandala of the ministers.
The altar for ordinary persons shall be eight cubits in length and breadth.
Upon it, one should fashion mudrās and images of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva as well as various mantra-deities.
It must not be identical to the rites for kings and ministers.
Upon that mandala, one should arrange the paths of the three realms, namely:
first white, second red, and third yellow.
One should use earthenware vessels; copper or silver may also be used.
According to one's means and according to one's faith,
one should employ flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, banners, canopies,
and all manner of ornaments; indeed, all such embellishments should be prepared.
One should also make offerings of various kinds of food and drink;
then, one should duly bestow upon them the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
Having entered and exited the maṇḍala according to the aforementioned ritual procedures, [the rite is concluded].
The World-Honored One, through skillful means for the sake of delivering sentient beings,
manifests various forms to liberate them.
Those who are to be delivered by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle—
To those who should be liberated by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle, he manifests in the form of a Śrāvaka to teach and transform them;
to those who should be liberated by means of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle,
he manifests in the form of a Pratyekabuddha to teach and transform them.
To those who are to be delivered by means of the Mahāyāna,
he manifests in the form of a bodhisattva to teach and transform them;
to those who are to be delivered by means of dhāraṇī-mantras, [he manifests accordingly].
Then he shall preach the Dharma for them so that they may abide in the wholesome paths;
regarding this, you must not give rise to doubt,
whether it be what the Buddha has spoken or what the Bodhisattvas have spoken.
The dhāraṇī methods and the methods for receiving and upholding mantras;
the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, and pratyekabuddhahood.
This continues until the realization of unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, one should know that those who enter the maṇḍala obtain a great accumulation of the fruits of merit.
Bodhisattvas who enter the maṇḍala attain wisdom.
In whatever place they are born, they shall attain the knowledge of past lives,
as well as supernatural powers and non-retrogression;
they shall ascend to the ten stages, transcend the realm of Māra, and be invincible.
All enemies and all karmic obstructions shall be completely extinguished.
The five sins of immediate retribution shall be swiftly eradicated.
One shall obtain such merit as this.
Furthermore, one shall obtain immeasurable accumulations of merit.
The thirteenth chapter, "The Chapter on Entering the Maṇḍala," is finished.
Chapter Fourteen: The Subjugation of Nāgas, the King of Mantra-Kings of the Amoghapāśa Lord of Light. If one wishes to subjugate nāgas:
One should proceed to the place where the dragon-dwelling pond is located.
At the edge of that pond, one should smear the ground with cow dung to form an altar.
Upon the altar, one should scatter flowers and burn incense such as sandalwood and aloeswood.
One should recite the Heart-King Mantra of the Blessed One, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s Amoghapāśa, one hundred and eight times.
When the one hundred and eight recitations are complete:
The water in that pond completely dried up.
All the nāgas and nāga-girls therein appeared before him with joyful expressions.
With the three karmas stilled, one should prostrate and say:
"Welcome, Noble One; what may your command be?
Then one should reply: "Whatever I intend, you shall perform."
At that time, the nāga and his nāga daughter spoke again, saying:
"Venerable One, please inform us of whatever you require.
The mantra-practitioner then replied:
"When I have business and think of you,
you should come to me at the proper time.
Then he replied, "I shall do as commanded."
Having spoken thus, he prostrated.
At that moment, the water in the pond returned to its full capacity, even exceeding its usual level.
He then entered it and returned to his own palace.
From this day forward, I shall constantly keep [this] in mind and never dare to forget it.
O Noble One, please do not punish me;
do not cause me to lose my sovereign power as a nāga deity.
He does not dare to be negligent regarding sensual desires,
fearing death and the prospect of falling into the evil realms.
Such is the practitioner of mantras.
Out of a desire to benefit all sentient beings, he called that nāga to mind;
as soon as he had called him to mind,
the nāga arrived immediately and vanished his nāga body.
With a divine and exquisite form like that of a youth,
and his body adorned with various ornaments,
he appeared before the mantra-practitioner, prostrated, and said:
"O Noble One, please grant me your instructions as to what you require and what I should do.
He should reply, "I require wealth and goods for the sake of providing for sentient beings who are poor and suffering."
Having seen him, I gave rise to a heart of great compassion.
Having heard this, I said:
"I shall surely fulfill his vow, just as the Noble One has instructed."
Then he enters the great ocean to retrieve the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi),
brings it forth, and says to the mantra-holder:
"This is the wish-fulfilling jewel."
It is able to remove the suffering of poverty for sentient beings;
according to their wishes, it bestows upon all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa food,
drink, and necessities, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
At that time, having received those jewels, the mantra-holder said, "Go back;
if I have need of you, remember me and come, do not forget.
Having obtained these pearls, he should gather immeasurable poor beggars.
Then, using flowers, incense, and flower garlands,
one should make offerings without letting anyone see them;
if anyone should see them, they will immediately vanish and no longer be obtainable.
Used with mastery, it transforms into a jewel worth one hundred koṭis;
if one were to sell it, one would obtain half that price.
If it is sold again and again as it is passed on, the price becomes progressively lower.
Finally, it was not valued at all;
lacking luster like a stone, it was cast aside.
Yet, when a Buddha appears in the world, his power of spiritual transformations [is such that]...
He returns once more to his original state, sinking back into the great ocean;
yet, by the power of his incantations and the power of his merit, he recovers this treasure.
Were it not for these, he would ultimately never obtain the dharma.
If it should happen that there is a drought in the world and crops fail to ripen, leading to famine,
one should again call him to mind; he will immediately come at the proper time,
appearing in the form of an ordinary person, and after paying homage, speak thus:
"Noble One, I have arrived; what shall I do?
He replied, "You should bring the five grains to maturity.
Having been thus instructed, by the supernatural power of the nāgas, at that very moment—
Rising into the void, he produced great black clouds;
the wind filled the sky and a heavy rain poured down.
When the heavy rain had sufficiently saturated the earth, the five grains reached full maturity.
Once the five grains had ripened, he spoke again with great earnestness:
"Noble One, I have already brought benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; what further remains to be done?
He should be told: "If I remember you again, you must return immediately."
Then the dragon, having received the instruction, paid his respects and departed, returning to his own palace.
Whenever he wished to see the world of the dragons, he would recollect it three times;
as soon as he had recollected it, [it appeared].
At that moment, he immediately appeared before the mantra-practitioner and said: "Noble One, I have now arrived.
I pray you grant me your instructions; what do you wish for me to do?"
He said, "Show me the world where the nāgas dwell.
As soon as he had spoken, he vanished from this place and arrived in the nāga world,
where he manifested that form through the power of the nāga deities.
The poisons of all nāgas cannot cause harm.
Just as the Naga Youth wanders through that world of nāgas without doubt or fear,
so too does he when he recollects the human world.
That nāga was about to provide divine and exquisite requisites,
superior and wonderful garments and various ornaments,
as well as divine and exquisite incense, flowers, and fine non-glutinous rice.
They possess exquisite celestial craftsmanship and enchanting songs such as are not found among humans;
having passed away from that realm, they have come to this human world.
The nāga immediately returned and requested three times,
saying, "Venerable One, what further task do you command me to perform?
The incantation-master told him what ought to be done.
"You have already completed your task; you may now depart.
Go as you please in peace and happiness, for you owe me nothing.
Having heard these words, he returned to his own palace by means of his nāga-supernatural power.
If one wishes to lead the nāga to another country,
the practitioner of the mantra should first perform the rite for protecting the body. Then,
proceeding to the nāga’s pond, he should recite this mantra.
The twenty-fifth mantra is as follows:
Oṃ (1) amogha (2) viśaya (3) mahānagna (4) panta panta (5) svāhā (6). This shall effect the binding of all directions.
There shall be no one capable of creating obstacles or causing disturbances.
One should construct a square altar;
if it is made of earth, it must be white and not a place where [the mantra] has previously been practiced or maintained.
Having prepared the altar by smearing it with ointments, scatter flowers and apply fragrant unguents.
Burn incense as an offering and draw a dragon-noose; do not simply draw a noose. This is not for a bodhisattva; recite the Amoghapāśa mantra one hundred and eight times.
One should step upon the dragon's head with the big toe of the right foot;
the dragon's body will become as hot as if it were being burned by fire,
