and it will then run out, no longer possessing any venom.
Bound and held fast by the power of the mantra-cord,
none of their supernatural powers can avail them;
even if they were to give vent to their wrath, it would be of no avail.
Then, the one who performs the snake-body incantation should take the dragon with his hand,
place it inside a basket or a wash-basin, and carry it away.
Wherever it is led, it follows along and ultimately cannot run away;
let it drink its milk and do not cause it to die.
If you wish to sell it, [take it with you].
If one sells [a dragon] in a land where there is no water, one incurs the offense of killing a dragon.
If, wishing to avoid this transgression, one brings it out of the water and establishes it for the benefit of all sentient beings, then there is no fault.
Once that nāga has settled there, he brings the five grains to maturity within that kingdom;
therefore, all the sentient beings of that country dwell in peace and happiness.
That land is prosperous and joyful, with a great multitude of people.
Rice, sugarcane, yellow cattle, and water buffaloes abound and flourish;
there is constant joy, with little illness and few troubles.
There is no pestilence, famine, or strife, nor are there wicked or rebellious thieves.
Fierce beasts remain hidden and cannot cause disturbance;
all those sentient beings are entirely virtuous and good,
being pure, honest, and upright, dwelling within the wholesome Dharma.
They always delight in giving and constantly cultivate joy;
they perform various meritorious deeds and steadfastly maintain the precepts of fasting;
and their mouths constantly proclaim such dharmas as suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impermanence.
In this remote borderland, there was no causeless rain, and floods and droughts were不调 (irregular).
Now, by the power of this dragon’s sustaining presence,
we have been liberated from these hardships.
That dragon also received great offerings and protected the kingdom.
Furthermore, he made a vow with him to receive the precepts.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, he was freed from the realm of animals and attained the stage of non-retrogression.
For that reciter of mantras, because he desires to benefit all sentient beings,
he attains the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā);
furthermore, this is due to his giving of life to sentient beings.
Therefore, one shall be freed from the realm of animals;
furthermore, it will not be difficult to advance toward the stage of Buddhahood.
This concludes the fourteenth chapter, "Subduing the Nāgas."

Chapter Fifteen: On the Visualization for the Accomplishment of the Sovereign King Amoghapāśa. At that time, if one wishes to serve the Sovereign King of Mantras, Amoghapāśa, [the following should be done].
That mantra-practitioner, having bathed for purification and donned fresh, clean garments,
shall observe the fast and precepts in a secluded place,
such as beneath a single tree or at a site containing the relics of a Buddha.
On the eighth or fourteenth day of the waxing moon,
prepare the site for the altar.
Before the altar, one should spread kuśa grass.
Sprinkle water upon the body and bind one's own topknot.
Having completed the protection of the body, recite this mantra as the twenty-sixth mantra.
The twenty-sixth mantra is as follows:
Oṃ amogha-pratihatā rākṣa rākṣa [insert one's own name] huṃ phaṭ svāhā. Recite this Amogha mantra three times over white mustard seeds and scatter them in the four directions.
All obstacles shall be completely extinguished, dispersed, and rendered incapable of causing disturbance.
One should sit in the full lotus posture, wrap the head with silk, form the yoga mudrā,
and recite the Amoghapāśa mantra one thousand and eight times.
When the full number of recitations is reached, there shall be a great sound,
as well as radiance and a rain of flowers.
The practitioner of the mantra must maintain a concentrated mind and not give way to fear.
It should be known that the attainment of the dharma-accomplishment of the King of Non-Emptiness is now complete.
Because of this manifestation of auspicious signs,
one should arise and make offerings with flowers, powdered incense, burning incense, and flower garlands.
With single-minded mindfulness, he observed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva as he surveyed the four directions.
Then, from the south, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva descended from the sky,
emitting hundreds of thousands of rays of light.
He is like a mass of fire riding upon clouds of dawn,
adorned with all manner of ornaments;
he has three eyes on his face, and his countenance is as dark-red as a jujube fruit.
The body has four arms, holding a flaming sword and grasping a lasso;
canine fangs protrude upward, and he wears crimson garments.
With a wrathful countenance, clouds of vapor issue from his nostrils.
His hands and feet were filled with gold, maṇi-jewels, vajras, and lapis lazuli;
he wore upon his head the terrifying form of a nāga king;
the King of Mantras laughed loudly, roaring and laughing again.
Just as the sound of a drum resounds through and clears away the mountain valleys, [the deity] will appear before that mantra-practitioner.
Let the practitioner not be afraid; simply recite the King of Mantras, the Amoghapāśa.
One should mentally recollect Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
scattering flowers and burning incense as an offering to him;
he will then appear in the sky in a form of joy.
With a celestial and wondrous body, manifesting his essential nature, he dwelt in tranquility and addressed the reciter of the mantra, saying:
"Excellent, O reciter! I am now filled with joy."
"What do you seek? Do you seek wealth and pleasure,
or do you seek to fly through the air as an Anuttara,
or the rank of a mantra-holding ṛṣi or a universal monarch?"
The Brahma King, Śakra, and the Four World-Protecting Kings seek the knowledge of past lives and the five supernormal powers;
[they seek] the fruit of stream-entry up to the fourth fruit.
This is the path of the Pratyekabuddhas, the unsurpassed Bodhisattvas,
and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the reciter shall fulfill whatever aspirations they desire.
Prostrate and supplicate for the fulfillment of the above wishes.
If they do not wish to comply, one should say,
"I shall rely upon you," and then follow their instructions and obey their commands.
They all act according to his commands; whatever is requested, they grant it.
Whatever objects are required by his mind, they bring them forth.
To whichever place he sends them, they depart according to his command.
If one wishes to go somewhere, it can take them there;
if they must come, it comes; and whatever is heard, it explains it all.
It constantly accompanies the Noble One in walking and staying.
If one does not wish for them to dwell near constantly,
they will come merely upon being recollected;
they will then manifest by bringing forth hidden treasures to show them.
It dispels all demonic possessions and is also able to punish them;
it removes all diseases and all deaths,
and it restrains fire, water, weapons, and poison.
Whether for praying for rain, stopping rain, restraining clouds, or restraining dragons—
whatever one desires shall all be accomplished.
If the practitioner of the mantra becomes angry, [the deity] will no longer manifest its form.
Therefore, the practitioner of mantras should protect both themselves and others;
they must not perform their intended actions without self-consecration,
nor should they be terrified.
Those who are indolent in their practice and engage in various evil deeds will find it difficult to achieve accomplishment and difficult even to behold [the results]. Therefore,
those who delight in merit and virtue should seek them with diligence.
Accomplishment is attained without effort.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, "The Visualization of the King of Non-Emptiness Accomplishment.
Chapter Sixteen: The Visualization of the Tathāgata Accomplishment, the King of Mantras of the Lord of Light, the Amoghapāśa. If one wishes to accomplish the visualization of the Tathāgata:
The practitioner of this mantra should practice the ten paths of wholesome action;
they should bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings and cultivate compassion with a mind of superior resolve.
Firmly persevering in one's vows, one makes offerings to the Triple Gem;
having completed these offerings,

one constructs a maṇḍala— translated here as a "platform"— before the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, using flowers, incense, burning perfumes, food and drink, and flower garlands, prepared according to one's means.
Having prepared all necessary requisites and offerings of lamps, and having completed the offerings,
one should observe the fast for either three days or seven days,
remaining pure and bathing at the three times of day.
Wearing new, clean garments— if one is a layperson, one should wear white clothes— and changing them at the three periods of the day,
one should sit in the full lotus posture upon an excellent and sublime seat,
form the seal of the Tathāgata, and simply recite the mantra.
While waiting, the body of the image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva vibrated;
manifesting supernatural powers, it then vanished from sight,
sometimes sitting upon a wheel, sometimes crouching, and sometimes standing.
Sometimes they manifest a single body, sometimes many bodies;
sometimes they manifest as coarse, sometimes as subtle;
or they emit radiance.
